title: All Roads Lead to Rome
objective: After this level you can explain how Roman roads were built and why they mattered.
summary: Layered, drained and as straight as the land allowed, over 80,000 km of main roads carried armies first, then everyone else.

cards.headline: Rome laid more than 80,000 km of main roads. Who were they for?
cards.body: Not for sightseeing. The answer explains why Romans built them so carefully, one layer at a time.

cards.headline: Built like a layer cake
cards.body: A major Roman road wasn’t just paving stones laid on dirt. It was stacked in layers: a foundation of large stones, then gravel or rubble, then paving stones on top. It ran as straight as the ground allowed, and it was cambered, curved slightly, so rainwater drained off instead of sitting in puddles. Next time you notice the gentle hump in the middle of a street, you’re looking at a Roman idea.
cards.callout: Camber: a slight curve that sheds water

cards.headline: Built for marching
cards.body: Roman roads were built first for the army. A straight, solid, well-drained road let legions march quickly. Remember the Via Appia from Level 19, begun in 312 BCE to move armies south? That was the model. But once a road existed, everyone used it: traders, officials and the imperial post. Built for boots, used by everyone.

cards.fact: Roman roads came with distance markers: milestones.
cards.context: Milestones along the roads marked distances in Roman miles, each 1,000 paces long. So a traveler could count down the stones to the next town, the way you watch the signs tick down on a highway today.

cards.headline: The roads: traveled
learned: They were cambered to drain rain
